ready1_open_rewrite.title: SciVerse open question
ready1_open_rewrite.rewritten_question_text: As shown in the figure, the liquid butane ($\mathrm{C_4H_{10}}$) sample in the pressurized lighter is placed directly below an aluminum can. The can contains 100.0 mL of water; when the butane is ignited, the water temperature in the can rises from 25.0°C to 82.3°C. The total mass of butane is found to be 0.51g, the specific heat capacity of water is 4.18J/(g·°C), and the density of water is 1.00g/mL. It is known that the density of butane at 25°C is 0.573g/mL. If 5.00 mL of butane is burned at this temperature, calculate the heat released (unit: kJ).

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, an aluminum beverage can can be seen placed on the metal mesh/ring of an iron stand, and a butane lighter is placed directly below the can; the fire source is used to heat the water in the can. Reasoning calculation: The volume of water is 100.0 mL, and the density is 1.00 g/mL, so the mass of water is 100.0 g. The temperature change is 82.3°C - 25.0°C = 57.3°C. The heat absorbed by the water q = mcΔT = 100.0 × 4.18 × 57.3 J = 23951.4 J = 23.9514 kJ. According to the calibration given in the problem, this is equivalent to the heat released by burning 0.51 g of butane and absorbed by the water. The mass of 5.00 mL of liquid butane at 25°C is 5.00 × 0.573 = 2.865 g. Scale up according to the mass ratio: q = 23.9514 × (2.865 / 0.51) kJ ≈ 134.5 kJ, rounded according to significant figures to about 1.3 × 10^2 kJ.
